**SECTION ONE: LOGIC**

*Read the passage below and answer the questions that follow:*

> One day on our way back from school, we met two of our classmates arguing over some stolen plums from a nearby farm. Paul wanted to get a greater share of the plums under the pretext that he was the one who climbed the plum tree. He said; If the owner saw them, he would be the one to take the blame. Then Peter retorted happily " that is fine, then take as much as you want because, if we are caught, then we will be penalized and if you take responsibility, then we will be penalised"
>
> As we are about to share the plums the owner of the farm appeared and shouted; "All students are thieves". They immediately ran off and left the plums.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a)

(i) Pick out a Categorical Proposition from the text. (1 mark)

(ii) Give the Subaltern of the Contrary of a (i) above. (2 marks)

(iii) What is the Contrapositive of a (ii)? (2 marks)

(iv) State the Truth-Value of the Contrariety of a (i). (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) A categorical proposition from the text (1 mark).** "All students are thieves" (the owner's shout). It is an **A-proposition** (universal affirmative): $\text{All } S \text{ are } P$, with $S$ = students and $P$ = thieves. It states without condition that one class is wholly included in another. The other sentences of the passage ("if we are caught, then we will be penalized...") are hypothetical (conditional) propositions, not categorical ones.

**(ii) The subaltern of the contrary of a (i) (2 marks).**
- The contrary of an A-proposition is the E-proposition with the same subject and predicate: **No students are thieves** (E).
- The subaltern of an E-proposition is the O-proposition (same subject, predicate and quality, but particular): **Some students are not thieves** (O).

**(iii) The contrapositive of a (ii) (2 marks).** Contraposition replaces the subject by the complement of the predicate and the predicate by the complement of the subject, keeping the quality. It is valid for A and O propositions. For the O-proposition "Some students are not thieves":
1. Obvert: Some students are non-thieves (I).
2. Convert: Some non-thieves are students (I).
3. Obvert: Some non-thieves are not non-students (O).

The contrapositive is therefore **"Some non-thieves are not non-students"** ($\text{Some non-}P \text{ are not non-}S$).

**(iv) The truth-value of the contrariety of a (i) (2 marks).** The contrariety is the relation between A and E: they cannot both be true, but they can both be false. So if "All students are thieves" is true, its contrary "No students are thieves" is **false**; if A were false, E would be undetermined (doubtful). Here the answer is **false** whichever way A is taken, because the passage itself shows that some students are thieves: Paul and Peter, two of the narrator's classmates, are arguing over stolen plums, so "No students are thieves" is false.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Using the terms "thieves" as minor term, "students" as middle term, and "responsible" as major term:

(i) Construct a valid syllogism in the Second Figure whose minor premise is an A-proposition. (3 marks)

(ii) State the mood of b(i). (1 mark)

(iii) Transform the syllogism in b(i) above into a Second Order Enthymeme. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The syllogism (3 marks).** Let $S$ = thieves (minor term), $M$ = students (middle term), $P$ = responsible persons (major term). In the **Second Figure** the middle term is the predicate of both premises: major premise $P - M$, minor premise $S - M$.

Which mood is possible? The middle term must be distributed at least once. In the Second Figure it is the predicate in both premises, and only a negative proposition distributes its predicate, so one premise must be negative, and therefore the conclusion is negative. Here the minor premise is an A (affirmative), so the major premise is the negative one. It must be universal (E), because an O major premise would not distribute $P$, which the negative conclusion distributes. This gives:

- Major premise (E): **No responsible persons are students.**
- Minor premise (A): **All thieves are students.**
- Conclusion (E): **Therefore, no thieves are responsible persons.**

Check of the rules: the middle term "students" is distributed in the major premise (predicate of an E); "responsible persons" is distributed in the major premise (subject of an E) and in the conclusion (predicate of an E); "thieves" is distributed in the conclusion and in the minor premise (subject of an A); there is exactly one negative premise and the conclusion is negative; there are three terms. The syllogism is valid (confirmed by a set-model check in Python: no assignment of sets makes the premises true and the conclusion false). Validity concerns the form, not the truth of the premises (the first premise is false in real life).

**(ii) The mood (1 mark).** The three propositions are E, A, E: the mood is **EAE**, in the Second Figure. This valid form is traditionally named **Cesare**.

**(iii) The Second Order Enthymeme (3 marks).** An enthymeme is a syllogism with one part left unstated. In a first-order enthymeme the major premise is suppressed, in a **second-order enthymeme the minor premise is suppressed**, and in a third-order enthymeme the conclusion is suppressed. Dropping the minor premise "All thieves are students" gives:

**No responsible persons are students; therefore, no thieves are responsible persons.**

(or, with the reason stated second: "No thieves are responsible persons, because no responsible persons are students").

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c)

(i) Identify a suitable proposition from the text that can be used to construct a Simple Constructive Dilemma. (1 mark)

(ii) Construct a Simple Constructive Dilemma using the proposition in c(i) above. (3 marks)

(iii) Refute c (ii) above by "Grasping the horns of the Dilemma". (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The suitable proposition (1 mark).** Peter's statement: **"If we are caught, then we will be penalized, and if you take responsibility, then we will be penalised."** It is a conjunction of two conditionals with the **same consequent** (we will be penalised), which is exactly the major premise of a *simple* constructive dilemma.

**(ii) The dilemma (3 marks).** The form of the Simple Constructive Dilemma is: $(p \supset r) \cdot (q \supset r)$, $\;p \vee q$, $\;\therefore r$. With $p$ = we are caught, $q$ = you (Paul) take responsibility, $r$ = we will be penalised:

- If we are caught, then we will be penalised, and if you take responsibility, then we will be penalised. $\;(p \supset r) \cdot (q \supset r)$
- Either we are caught or you take responsibility. $\;p \vee q$
- **Therefore, we will be penalised.** $\;\therefore r$

The dilemma is formally valid (checked by truth table): whichever disjunct holds, the same consequent follows.

**(iii) Refutation by grasping the horns (3 marks).** To grasp the horns of a dilemma is to deny the **major premise**, that is, to show that at least one of the two conditionals (the "horns") is false, so that the conjunction $(p \supset r) \cdot (q \supset r)$ is false. For example:

- Deny the second horn: "It is **not** true that if you take responsibility, then we will be penalised." Paul himself said that if the owner saw them he would be the one to take the blame; a person who takes responsibility accepts the blame himself, so the others need not be penalised. Hence $q \supset r$ is false.
- The first horn can also be denied: being caught does not by itself bring a penalty; the owner may simply recover the plums or forgive them. Hence $p \supset r$ may also be false.

Since the major premise is false, the argument does not establish that "we will be penalised", although its form is valid. (The other two ways of meeting a dilemma are escaping between the horns, by denying $p \vee q$, and rebutting it with a counter-dilemma.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d)

(i) Identify the Fallacy most clearly committed by the owner of the farm. (2 marks)

(ii) Explain how the Fallacy has been committed. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The fallacy (2 marks).** **Hasty generalisation** (also called the fallacy of converse accident, or sweeping generalisation): "All students are thieves".

**(ii) How it is committed (2 marks).** The owner has seen, at most, two students (Paul and Peter) taking plums, and from this very small and unrepresentative sample he draws a conclusion about **every** student, including the narrator's group and all students everywhere. What is true of a few members of a class is wrongly asserted of the whole class. The evidence (a few cases of stealing) can support at most "Some students are thieves" (an I-proposition); it cannot support the universal "All students are thieves" (an A-proposition). The statement is also unjust, since it condemns innocent students.
